procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 13, 1971 in Criminal Misc. Cases Nos. 169, 177, 222, 224, 229, 230, 231, 237, 285, 286, 287, 316, 328, 329, 330 and 331 of 1971.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court held that the Act in question was not a law made by Parliament in terms of Art. 22(7) of the Constitution. It further held that the provisions contained in ss. 11 and 13 of the Act relating to the procedure before the Advisory Board in respect of a person detained for a longer period than three months were ultra vires Art. 22(7) of the Constitution. The High Court concluded that Art. 19(1) was not applicable to the impugned Act and rejected the challenge based on Art. 14 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and set aside the judgment of the High Court. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to hear and dispose of the writ petitions on other points raised on the merits.

directions: The judgment of the High Court is set aside.
The writ petitions will now be heard and disposed of by the High Court on other points on the merits which require determination.

issue.issue_text: Whether the State Legislature is competent to make a law providing for preventive detention for a period longer than three months and prescribing the procedure for the Advisory Board, in the absence of a law made by Parliament under Article 22(7) of the Constitution.

facts: The High Court had ruled that a State Legislature was incompetent to make a law providing for preventive detention for more than three months or to prescribe the procedure for the Advisory Board.
The High Court's reasoning was that under Article 22(7) of the Constitution, Parliament alone has the jurisdiction to legislate on these matters.
The State appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.
law: Article 22(7) of the Constitution is a permissive and enabling provision, not a mandatory one. It authorizes Parliament to make laws on certain aspects of preventive detention but does not impose an obligatory duty to do so.

Under Article 246 and Entry 3 of List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule, both Parliament and State Legislatures have concurrent and co-extensive powers to make laws regarding preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State and public order.

A State law on a concurrent subject is valid unless it conflicts with a law made by Parliament on the same matter (Article 254). The absence of a Parliamentary law does not act as a bar on the State's legislative power.
Article 22(4) prohibits detention beyond three months unless an Advisory Board has reported sufficient cause for such detention.
application: The Court rejected the argument that Article 22(7) confers exclusive jurisdiction on Parliament. It held that the clause merely gives Parliament an "overriding power" but does not prohibit the State Legislature from acting.

The Court reasoned that since State Legislatures have plenary and co-extensive power with Parliament on this subject (under the Concurrent List), they are competent to legislate on all incidental matters, including the period of detention and the procedure for the Advisory Board.
The Court found no provision in the Constitution that would limit the State's power to make a law for detention beyond three months simply because Parliament had not passed a law on the subject.

It concluded that a State Legislature can make a law for preventive detention for a period longer than three months, provided it includes the safeguard of obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board as required by Article 22(4).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the argument that the State Legislature is competent to make a law providing for preventive detention for a period longer than three months and to prescribe the procedure for the Advisory Board, even in the absence of a specific law made by Parliament under Article 22(7). The Court held that the State's power is derived from the Concurrent List and is not limited by the mere absence of a Parliamentary law on the subject.

issue.issue_text: Whether the word 'may' in the opening part of Article 22(7) of the Constitution must be read as 'shall', making it mandatory for Parliament to legislate on the matters specified therein.

law.law_text: Article 22(7) of the Constitution states that Parliament 'may' by law prescribe certain matters related to preventive detention, such as the circumstances for detention beyond three months and the maximum period of detention.
The Court cited its previous decisions in S. Krishnan v. State of Madras and Gopalan v. State of Madras, which had already held that Article 22(7)(b) is permissive, not mandatory.

application.explanation: The Supreme Court interpreted the word 'may' in Article 22(7) according to its plain and normal meaning, concluding that it is an enabling or permissive provision, not a mandatory one. It merely authorizes or enables Parliament to make a law on the specified subjects but does not impose an obligation to do so.

The Court rejected the respondent's argument that 'may' should be read as 'shall' for sub-clauses (b) and (c) while remaining permissive for sub-clause (a). The Court found no principle or precedent to support such an inconsistent interpretation without compelling reasons.
The Court relied on binding precedent from earlier cases (S. Krishnan and Gopalan), which had already established that the provision was permissive.

The Court also reasoned that if the Constitution had intended to limit the power of State Legislatures to make laws for detention beyond three months in the absence of a Parliamentary law, it would have included an express provision to that effect. The absence of such a limitation supported the view that the power granted to Parliament in Article 22(7) was not exclusive or a mandatory prerequisite for state action.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the word 'may' in Article 22(7) is permissive and enabling, not mandatory. Therefore, it does not compel Parliament to legislate on the matters specified therein.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned Act is violative of Article 19(1) of the Constitution.

facts: The West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970 was challenged on the grounds that the restrictions it imposed on a detenu's rights under Article 19(1)(d) (the right to move freely throughout the territory of India) were unreasonable.
The petitioners argued that these restrictions were not in the interest of the general public and therefore the Act should be struck down.
law: The Court acknowledged that after the decision in Cooper's case, the reasonableness of restrictions imposed by a preventive detention law could be tested against Article 19.
Restrictions on the fundamental right to freedom of movement under Article 19(1)(d) can be justified if they are in the interest of the general public.
application: The Supreme Court took "judicial notice" of the historical events in West Bengal that led to the imposition of President's rule.
The Court reasoned that these events demonstrated a clear necessity for the Act to be enacted in the interest of the general public.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the restrictions on citizens' freedom placed by the Act were "eminently in the interest of the general public." Consequently, the Court rejected the challenge and found that the Act was not violative of Article 19(1) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned Act is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.

facts: The Act was challenged on the ground that it was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
The specific argument was that the Act gave arbitrary, unguided, and uncanalised power to the State Executive without prescribing any guidelines for its exercise.
law: Article 14 of the Constitution provides for equality before the law and prohibits unreasonable classification by the state.
application: The Court examined the classification of persons and activities contemplated by the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court repelled the challenge, holding that the classification contemplated by the Act could not be considered unreasonable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the State Legislature is competent to make a law providing for preventive detention for a period longer than three months and prescribing the procedure for the Advisory Board, in the absence of a law made by Parliament under Article 22(7) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: Article 22(7) of the Constitution does not confer exclusive jurisdiction on Parliament to legislate on preventive detention for periods longer than three months.
The State Legislature is fully competent to make laws for detention, to prescribe the procedure for the Advisory Board, and to authorize detention beyond three months.
respondent_arguments: The State Legislature is not competent to make a law for preventive detention for more than three months without a law being made by Parliament under Article 22(7). (Inferred from the High Court's judgment which was in their favor and being appealed).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the word 'may' in the opening part of Article 22(7) of the Constitution must be read as 'shall', making it mandatory for Parliament to legislate on the matters specified therein.
appellant_arguments: The word 'may' is permissive and does not impose a mandatory obligation on Parliament to legislate. (Inferred as the counter-argument to the respondent's contention).
respondent_arguments: The word 'may' in the opening part of Article 22(7) must be read as 'shall', making it a mandatory duty for Parliament to legislate on the matters specified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the impugned Act is violative of Article 19(1) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The impugned Act is constitutionally valid and does not violate Article 19(1). (Inferred as the defense against the respondent's challenge).
respondent_arguments: The impugned Act is violative of Article 19(1), especially in light of the decision in R. C. Cooper v. Union of India.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the impugned Act is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The impugned Act is not violative of Article 14. (Inferred as part of the general defense of the Act's constitutionality).
respondent_arguments: The impugned Act is violative of Article 14. (Inferred as part of the 'general argument challenging the vires of the Act').

cases.case_name: S. Krishnan v. State of Madras
cases.principle: To support the conclusion that the general argument challenging the vires (validity) of the Act was without substance.
To support the conclusion that the general argument challenging the vires (validity) of the Act was without substance.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For an act's provisions to be valid, there must be a fairly close and rational nexus between the acts covered by its clauses and the maintenance of public order and the security of the State.
obiter: A court can and should take judicial notice of historical events which demonstrate the necessity of a law in the interest of the general public.
A disturbance of public order in a State may in turn prejudicially affect its security.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The restrictions on a citizen's freedom of movement imposed by the impugned preventive detention Act are constitutionally valid as they are eminently in the interest of the general public. The Court took judicial notice of the historical events leading to President's rule in the state, which demonstrated the necessity for such an Act to maintain public order and the security of the State. The various clauses of the Act have a close and rational nexus to these objectives.
legal_tests_applied: Rational Nexus Test: The court examined whether there was a 'Fairly close and rational nexus' between the acts proscribed by the statute (e.g., those in s. 3(2)) and the legislative objective of maintaining public order and security of the State.

Narrow Construction to Uphold Constitutionality: To save a statutory provision from being unconstitutional, the court will adopt a restricted construction if the language permits. The court applied this to Section 3(2)(c) by 'legitimately imputing to the law-maker the intention to enact a valid provision of law within the constitutional limitations', thereby construing the act of 'insult' to apply only to public acts capable of disturbing public order.

Judicial Notice of Historical Context: The court can and should take 'judicial notice of the historical events' surrounding the enactment of a law to determine if the restrictions it imposes are necessary and in the public interest.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the Act violated Article 19(1)(d) was rejected because the court found the restrictions to be in the interest of the general public, citing the historical context of President's rule as justification for the law's necessity.

The challenge to the specific clauses (a), (b), (d), and (e) of Section 3(2) of the Act was deemed 'prima facie unfounded' as the acts covered by these clauses were reasonably likely to be prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.

The respondent's argument that insulting the national flag in private (under clause (c)) has no nexus with public order was defeated by the court's narrow construction of the clause. The court held it must be interpreted to mean an insult caused 'in such a situation as reasonably exposes the act... to the public view' and is 'capable of arousing the feelings of indignation in someone', thus establishing a connection to the maintenance of public order.
The general challenge to the vires of the Act was dismissed as being 'wholly without substance'.
policy_considerations: Security of a State, maintenance of public order, and of supplies and services essential to the community demand effective safeguards in the larger interest of sustenance of peaceful democratic way of life.
